Defendant: YIP PAK KEUNG (also known as BENJAMIN YIP)

facts.F2: The Defendant (D) filed a defence on 19 October 2018, claiming that the agreements were investment agreements with no obligation to repay.
facts.F3: D raised the issue of illegality and denied the relevant representations.

facts.F7: Allowing the amendment would necessitate further amendments to P's Reply.

facts.F9: Further amendments to P's Reply would necessitate further witness statements.
facts.F10: The proposed amendment would affect trial/milestone dates and divert P's preparation.
facts.F11: If the amendment were allowed, P would need to incur time and effort to deal with the newly pleaded limitation defence.
facts.F12: Allowing the amendment would prejudice P's preparation for trial.

reference_issues: Whether the limitation defence should be allowed to be amended into the defence at this late stage

facts.F1: The plaintiff was born in 1928 in Canton, China and married young to an engineer named Lee. She came to Hong Kong in 1954 with her son Dick after her husband's arrest and imprisonment.
facts.F2: The plaintiff met Fung Shing Ting in 1957 and they cohabited together, going through a Chinese marriage ceremony. Fung was still married to his first wife, Ivy Hung.
facts.F3: The plaintiff and Fung had a son, Dick, who changed his surname to Fung and went to school in Hong Kong. However, the family could not live together due to constant friction between Fung and Dick.
facts.F4: In 1968, the plaintiff married an English airman and left Hong Kong, but returned in 1972 and started a Bed and Breakfast business with her son.
facts.F5: In 1975, Fung was released from Castle Peak Hospital and promised the plaintiff that he would live with her in the Flat as man and wife, and that she would be entitled to the Flat after his death.
facts.F6: The plaintiff spent money on renovating the Flat and reconnecting utilities, and Fung made a Chinese Will in 1981 leaving the Flat to her.
facts.F7: Fung had repeated discussions, understandings, and arrangements with the plaintiff about the Flat.
facts.F8: Fung died in 1986, and the plaintiff claimed that she was entitled to the Flat based on the Chinese Will and the promises made by Fung.
facts.F9: The plaintiff altered her position in reliance on the agreements with Fung.
facts.F10: The plaintiff had a belief that she would be given the Flat, which was encouraged by Fung, and she relied on this belief to her detriment.

facts.F5: The Building is governed by a Deed of Mutual Covenant dated 3 June 1966 and under the First Schedule of it, each of the units in the Building is allocated 1/16 undivided shares.
facts.F6: The respondents, KWOK HON PON and TSUI WAI YING, filed a Form 33 (Notice of Opposition) asserting that redevelopment was not justified, and the offers and valuation were too low.
facts.F7: The Notice of Opposition and all evidence filed in opposition, including witness statements and expert evidence, were withdrawn by consent.
facts.F8: The applicants, owning all the undivided shares of the Lot save those 2/16 allotted to Flat 1B and Flat 5A respectively, were entitled to file the Application under section 3(1) of the Ordinance.
facts.F9: The applicants had imposed a condition that R1 & R2 have to give good title of Flat A, but R1 & R2 are unable to procure R3-6 to do so.
facts.F10: The Building has been suffering from various deteriorations resulted from unauthorized building works, substandard workmanship, lack of repair, and continuous natural weathering over the years.
facts.F11: The applicants proposed to appoint Mr Ma Ho Fai and Ms Kung Ying Chang as the sale trustees.
facts.F12: The applicants prepared a set of draft Particulars and Conditions of Sale of the Lot.
facts.F13: The Tribunal relied on the expert evidence of Mr Benson Wong and Mr C M Wong in determining that redevelopment of the Building is justified due to its age and state of repair.
facts.F14: The Tribunal considered the applicants' effort in achieving settlements with the various respondents.
facts.F15: A valuation report was prepared by Mr Chan to determine the reserve price of the Lot.

claim: Claims damages under the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provision) Ordinance and the Fatal Accidents Ordinance
requested_remedy: Claims damages under the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provision) Ordinance and the Fatal Accidents Ordinance
parties: Plaintiff: Mrs. Kwan Kwong (widow of Kwan Kwong and administratrix of his estate)
Defendant: First defendant (driver of truck numbered AD6025), Second defendant (owner of truck numbered AD6025)

facts.F1: Kwan Kwong, a 56-year-old interior decorator, was walking in Tin Lok Lane on March 1st, 1968.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff's husband, Kwan Kwong, was knocked down by a truck numbered AD6025 and died from his injuries on March 2nd, 1968.
facts.F3: Wong Tong, an independent witness, saw the accident occur and testifies that the truck did not stop after hitting Kwan Kwong.
facts.F4: Ho Chi, a workmate of Kwan Kwong, corroborates Wong Tong's evidence about the truck's actions.
facts.F5: The first defendant admitted to driving the truck down Tin Lok Lane but claimed not to have seen or hit Kwan Kwong.
facts.F6: Kwan Kwong had seven children with his wife, but only the three youngest were dependents.
facts.F7: Kwan Kwong earned about $700 per month and gave his wife $500 for household expenses.
facts.F8: The family lived together but Kwan Kwong was often absent due to work and did not contribute much to household expenses.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff lives in a household supported partly by her children, and she receives occasional contributions from the eldest three.
facts.F10: The first defendant was not keeping proper lookout at the time of the accident.
facts.F11: The truck was properly identified as the one involved in the accident.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff is entitled to damages for funeral expenses, loss of expectation of life, and dependency under the two Ordinances.
facts.F13: The court applied a multiplier to assess the total dependency to determine the damages under the Fatal Accidents Ordinance.

reference_issues: Whether the first defendant's truck caused the accident that resulted in Kwan Kwong's death.
Whether the first defendant was at fault for the accident.
The Plaintiff's entitlement to damages under the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provision) Ordinance and the Fatal Accidents Ordinance.

claim: Damages for loss of dependency and loss of expectation of life under Fatal Accidents Ordinance (FAD) and Law Amendment & Reform (Consolidation) Ordinance (LARCO)
requested_remedy: Damages for loss of dependency and loss of expectation of life under Fatal Accidents Ordinance (FAD) and Law Amendment & Reform (Consolidation) Ordinance (LARCO)
parties: Plaintiff: WONG Yat-chee's mother (administratrix of WONG Yat-chee's estate)

facts.F1: The deceased, WONG Yat-chee, died on 1st May 1978 in a taxi accident at the age of 21.
facts.F2: The accident occurred when the taxi veered onto the opposite carriageway and collided with an oncoming taxi on Prince Edward Road flyover.
facts.F3: The deceased was a passenger in the taxi and sustained multiple injuries, resulting in his death.
facts.F4: The plaintiff, WONG Yat-chee's mother, is the administratrix of his estate.
facts.F5: At the time of his death, the deceased was the sole contributor to the family, providing $800 per month to support his mother and two younger brothers.
facts.F6: The deceased was engaged to be married and had registered his proposed marriage, but had assured his mother that he would continue to contribute to the family despite getting married.
facts.F7: The family consisted of the mother, WONG Yat-chee, and his three brothers, WONG Chun-shing, WONG Chi-keung, and WONG Yat-ting.
facts.F8: The eldest brother, WONG Chun-shing, was not reliant on WONG Yat-chee's contributions.
facts.F9: The two younger brothers, WONG Chi-keung and WONG Yat-ting, were reliant on WONG Yat-chee's contributions.
facts.F10: The mother had never asked WONG Yat-chee about his income, but he had given her and his brothers financial support.
facts.F11: After WONG Yat-chee's death, the family's financial situation changed, with the eldest son taking on work to support the family and the mother starting work sorting plastic waste.
facts.F12: The court considered the ages and personal circumstances of the dependants in assessing damages.
facts.F13: The deceased's working life expectancy would have involved vicissitudes and possibilities of expenditure, which the court took into account when assessing damages for lost years.

Assessment of damages for loss of expectation of life
Assessment of damages for lost years
